summary: A BBN memo about problems with Telnet, the remote terminal protocol, starting from the question of who should echo typed characters. The authors work down to underlying principles and propose an alternative scheme for echoing. It is a design discussion that fed into later Telnet meetings, not a final specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 435 discusses who should display the characters a Telnet user types. It proposes that either side can request an echo mode and gives a short negotiation procedure intended to avoid loops.

questions: what is no echo in telnet
subtitle: A discussion of Telnet echoing and broader principles for negotiating options.

tldr.problem: The authors found that Telnet's echo conventions made users and servers accommodate the wrong echo mode and required users to remember each server's preferred setup.
tldr.mechanism: They propose that either side may request ECHO or NO ECHO, with a defined default and acknowledgments that limit negotiation to three commands.
tldr.outcome: RFC 435 is a discussion memo proposing an echo scheme and broader ideas about defaults, negotiated options, and symmetry. It is not a final specification.

sections.title: The Echoing Problem
sections.content:
RFC 435 discusses Telnet issues, beginning with echoing: whether the user's terminal or the remote server displays the characters the user types. The authors say servers seemed optimized for terminals that either echo themselves or do not, and that the existing conventions prevented a server from initiating a change in echo mode.

The authors argue this can burden servers with users in an unsuitable mode and require users to remember the right setup for each server. They also say hiding input is separate from echoing and recommend a distinct STOP HIDING YOUR INPUT command rather than using NO ECHO for both functions.
sections.plainLanguage: Echoing decides whether the local terminal or remote server shows typed characters. The authors say users should not have to remember a different echo setup for every server.

sections.title: The Proposed Echo Negotiation
sections.content:
The proposal allows both the server and the user to suggest an echo mode. When sent by the server, ECHO means “I will echo to you”; when sent by the user, it means “you echo to me.” The meaning of NO ECHO also depends on which side sends it.

A connection begins in NO ECHO mode. Either side may request a change, but changes only take effect when the recipient accepts the request as an available mode. The recipient acknowledges a change or refuses it with the inverse command. The authors say that no matter who starts, at most three commands pass between the parties, so the procedure cannot loop.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection starts with no remote echo. Either side can request a change, and the other side confirms or refuses it using the proposed rules.

sections.title: Defaults, Negotiation, and Symmetry
sections.content:
The authors identify three principles: default implementation, negotiated options, and symmetry. A default must be implemented for every option; both parties must agree before using an option; and neither party should need to know whether it is the server or the user.

The memo applies these principles to possible options beyond echoing, including line-at-a-time input, end-of-line conventions, hiding input, character sets, and a QUOTE character for binary data. It sketches command prefixes such as WILL, WON'T, DO, and DON'T, and says a host could support a default mode while refusing options it does not understand. These are broader proposals, not a completed Telnet specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo argues that each option should have a default and should be used only after agreement. It also proposes making the rules work similarly for either side of a connection.

sections.title: A Sample TIP Implementation
sections.content:
The appendix sketches a TIP implementation that tracks three state bits for each terminal: P for the terminal's physical echo capability, D for the user's desired mode, and A for the mode currently used by the connection. When a terminal connects, the TIP sets these values and starts the connection in NO ECHO mode.

When a request arrives, the TIP compares the request with the terminal's capability and the user's preference. It changes the actual mode only when allowed and acknowledges or refuses as described in the proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: The example TIP remembers what the terminal can do, what the user wants, and what the connection currently does. It uses those three values to decide whether to accept an echo request.
